mcqs.question: A cloud storage bucket is public by default unless an administrator explicitly locks it down, even though locking it down takes only one setting change. Why does this still count as a secure-defaults failure?
options: Because most users take the default behavior as-is rather than deliberately configuring either option, so whatever the default is becomes the behavior most deployments actually ship with
Because locking down a bucket is technically more difficult than making it public
Because public buckets are always technically more secure than private ones
Because cloud providers never allow buckets to be made private after creation
mcqs.explanation: The core insight is that effort predicts behavior — even if the safe option is just as easy to select, most users won't deliberately choose either option, they'll accept whatever ships as the default, so the default itself is what determines real-world outcomes at scale. Locking down isn't harder than the public default, public buckets aren't more secure, and buckets can be made private after creation.

mcqs.question: An authorization check throws an exception because a downstream permission service is unreachable. What does "fail-safe" (fail-closed) mean in this situation?
options: The system should retry the check indefinitely until it succeeds
The system should log the error but take no action on the request itself
The system should escalate to a human reviewer before responding
The system should treat the inability to evaluate the check as a denial, rather than allowing the request to proceed
mcqs.explanation: Fail-safe specifically means treating an unevaluated check as a 'no' — the request is denied rather than allowed through by default, which is the correct posture for most security-relevant decisions. Indefinite retries, silent logging with no action, and human escalation are all different (and not necessarily wrong) design choices, but none of them define what fail-safe itself means.

mcqs.question: Framework A enables CSRF protection on every form by default, requiring an explicit exemption for endpoints that don't need it. Framework B requires developers to explicitly enable CSRF protection per form. Which is the healthier default pattern, and why?
options: Framework B, because opt-in security gives developers more control
Neither — CSRF protection should never be handled at the framework level
Framework B, because opt-in features are always more performant
Framework A, because the protected state is the path of least resistance, and skipping it requires a deliberate, visible action a code reviewer can notice and question
mcqs.explanation: When protection is on by default, every developer who does nothing extra still gets it, and disabling it is the visible, deliberate action — which is exactly the opt-in-to-disable pattern this slide favors over opt-in-to-enable. Framework-level handling is a legitimate and common approach, opt-in security doesn't meaningfully improve developer control in a way that outweighs the coverage gap, and there's no inherent performance difference between the two patterns.

mcqs.question: A rate limiter is deliberately designed to fail open (allow traffic through unthrottled) if its own backing infrastructure becomes unavailable. Why might this be a defensible choice, unlike failing open on an authorization check?
options: Because rate limiting has no legitimate purpose and can be safely ignored

Because the rate limiter's own outage taking down the entire protected service is judged worse than temporarily allowing unthrottled traffic, whereas an authorization bypass directly grants unauthorized access
Because fail-open is always the correct choice for every kind of check
Because rate limiters cannot technically be implemented to fail closed
mcqs.explanation: The classification matters: rate limiting protects availability, so its own failure mode is weighed against a different availability risk, while authorization protects against unauthorized access directly, making an accidental bypass a security failure rather than a availability trade-off. Rate limiting does serve a real purpose, fail-open isn't universally correct, and rate limiters can technically be built to fail closed — this is a deliberate choice, not a technical constraint.

mcqs.question: When auditing a codebase for accidental fail-open behavior, what should a reviewer specifically look for beyond just checking whether the "check passes" and "check fails" paths deny access correctly?
options: Whether the check function has a sufficiently descriptive name
Whether the check is called more than once per request
What happens on every other exit path — the check throwing an exception, timing out, or its dependency becoming unreachable — since a bare catch block can silently treat these as permission granted
Whether the check uses synchronous or asynchronous code
mcqs.explanation: Accidental fail-open almost never comes from broken pass/fail logic — it comes from an unhandled or mishandled error path where the surrounding code proceeds as if permission had been granted, which is exactly the exit path a pass/fail-only review misses. Function naming, call frequency, and sync-vs-async style are unrelated to whether an error path silently grants access.

mcqs.question: A developer wraps a permission check in a try/catch that sets `allowed = True` if the permission service throws an exception, specifically to stop the request from crashing. What is the actual effect of this code during a real outage of that service?
options: Every request through this code path becomes silently unauthorized, since any error from the permission service is treated as a granted permission
The request is safely denied whenever the permission service is unreachable
The application will refuse to start until the permission service is reachable
The code has no effect on authorization outcomes, only on logging
mcqs.explanation: Setting `allowed = True` in the exception handler means any failure to reach or evaluate the permission service is treated identically to an explicit grant — exactly the accidental fail-open pattern this pitfall describes, with a blast radius as wide as the outage itself. This is the opposite of a safe denial, it doesn't block application startup, and it directly determines authorization outcomes, not just logging.
